clue.text: Indulgent acts — son's fitting vindication?

indicators.note: fitting is read as fitting together, assembling the letters of the preceding words in a new order

parts.note: son's stands for son is, so only the word son goes into the mix

explanation.surface: A grown son, caught out in some indulgence, claims his behaviour is justified because everything was agreed.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: the letters of INDULGENT ACTS SON are rearranged, and the full sentence hints at the plea a grown-up son might make.
explanation.definitionFit: Consenting adults are grown-ups who agree to private conduct, the classic legal defence for indulgent behaviour between willing parties.

clue.text: Eccentric relation from Shanghai?

indicators.note: eccentric means odd or off-centre, telling us the letters of relation are set out oddly

explanation.surface: An oddball family member who happens to come from a city in China.
explanation.definitionFit: Shanghai is in East Asia, and oriental is an old adjective for things from the East; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: On-board facility where crew may purchase Romulan Ale?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a key on a keyboard, the board here being a computer's

definitions.text: where crew may purchase Romulan Ale?
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a drinking spot on a starship; Romulan Ale is a drink in Star Trek

explanation.walkthrough: The picture is a bar on a spaceship serving Star Trek's Romulan Ale, but the facility on the board is the long key that types a gap.
explanation.definitionFit: The long key at the bottom of a computer keyboard inserts a gap between words, and the phrase also reads as a starship's pub.

clue.text: Set up to get this party out following Johnson's latest shambles

indicators.note: following means the rest comes after the letter from Johnson
latest means the final letter, so the last of Johnson's is taken

parts.note: last letter of Johnson

indicators.note: set up in a down clue lifts the word to so it reads from the bottom upwards
out means put out of order, so the letters of get this party are jumbled

explanation.surface: A political plot to oust a party after Boris Johnson's final mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set up' works because this is a down clue, so a reversed word reads upwards; Johnson is just a name whose last letter is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A shambles is an ugly mess, and calling something an unappealing spectacle is the idiomatic way to describe one.

clue.text: Heading from stable for new location after such a declaration?

definitions.text: Heading from stable for new location after such a declaration?

parts.words: Heading from stable for new location after such a declaration?
parts.note: after someone declares they are ravenous enough to eat a whole animal, that animal would head from its stable to the dinner table; dropping the head of stable gives table

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a horse being moved to new stables, but the new location is the table, which is stable with its first letter gone.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the idiomatic boast of someone who is extremely hungry, and the clue imagines it taken literally.

clue.text: Famous last words of High Court Judge

definitions.text: Famous last words of High Court Judge

parts.words: Famous last words of High Court Judge
parts.note: the judge is a tennis umpire perched on a high chair beside the court, whose final call ends a match

explanation.walkthrough: A High Court Judge suggests a senior legal figure, but the court is a tennis court and the judge the umpire in the high chair.
explanation.definitionFit: The tennis umpire announces this phrase when the final point is won, so it is literally the last thing said.

clue.text: Club auditor's finished letter you provided with title

indicators.note: an auditor is a listener, so what follows is how the words sound when heard

parts.words: finished letter you provided with title
parts.note: finished means done; the letter D is spelt dee; taken as written for its sound; given a title like Sir, that is knighted

explanation.surface: An accountant has completed a letter, and a reader has been given a title.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, DONE DEE YOU KNIGHTED gives the club's name; the auditor seems to be a financial checker but is just a listener.
explanation.definitionFit: Dundee United is a Scottish football club based in the city of Dundee.

clue.text: Harry is the current kid in the way

indicators.note: to harry is to harass or disturb, so the letters of is the current are disturbed

explanation.surface: Someone called Harry is the latest child to get under people's feet.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry looks like a name, but it is the verb meaning to harass, which signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A street urchin is a ragged child who lives on the streets, so a kid in the way in the road sense.

clue.text: See 1
I delivered to Carlton fresh coriander

indicators.note: fresh means new, so the letters are made into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone drops off fresh herbs to a man called Carlton, or the Carlton hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fresh' seems to describe the coriander but signals rearranging I with CARLTON.
explanation.definitionFit: Cilantro is the American name for the leaves of the coriander plant, used as a herb.

clue.text: Izzard and Murphy put together quick turns

definitions.meaning: first meaning: comedians Eddie Izzard and Eddie Murphy taken as a pair share a first name
second meaning: whirls of water or air, swirling currents

explanation.surface: Two comedians combine for a quick-fire double act of short routines.
explanation.definitionFit: Two comics named Eddie make a plural of the name, and the same word means small whirlpools that spin round fast.

clue.text: Sniffer dog circling leader of local crime organisation

indicators.note: circling means the dog's letters go round, so its opening pair is carried round to the end

parts.note: a pointer is a gun dog that scents game

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of local

explanation.surface: A police sniffer dog circles the head of a local gang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circling' sends the dog's first two letters round to its tail before the L from 'leader of local' is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Interpol is the international police body that coordinates action against crime across borders.

clue.text: Inside of each aircraft controls carbon emissions

indicators.note: inside of says what follows sits within the letters for each

parts.note: EA is the standard abbreviation for each, as in price lists

indicators.note: controls is read as holds, so the aircraft holds the carbon inside it

parts.note: a jet is an aircraft
C is the chemical symbol for carbon

explanation.surface: Engine controls on each plane regulate its carbon output.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside of' looks like a call for a word's middle letters, but it puts the aircraft, holding carbon, inside the abbreviation for each.
explanation.definitionFit: Ejecta is material thrown out, as by a volcano or star, so it names matter that has been emitted.

clue.text: Admin time: first by single worker, then by more than one

parts.note: one worker is a man
an age is a period of time; the clue reuses time as its abbreviation T in the second half
more than one worker gives men
then carries the clue's time on into the second half, this time as its abbreviation T

explanation.surface: A job advert for office time, first a lone worker then a team.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says time once but uses it twice: as a period after the lone worker, then abbreviated after the group of workers.
explanation.definitionFit: Management is the running and administration of an organisation, and also its administrators collectively.

clue.text: Strain of A2: AS taken and a Uni arranged, fine student cracks

indicators.note: cracks means breaks into, so the following pair goes inside
arranged means put in a new order, so the letters of a and Uni are rearranged

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil grades
L for learner, a student driver's plate

explanation.surface: An exam-board breakdown: AS levels, A2 and a university course, with a fine student cracking.
explanation.walkthrough: A2 and AS sound like British school exams, but A2 here is the influenza subtype H2N2. 'Arranged' turns A UNI into IANU, which F and L crack open.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1957 pandemic called Asian flu was caused by the influenza A subtype H2N2, so it is a strain of that virus.

clue.text: Wear fancy dress/college uniform — suspicion remains

parts.note: U is uniform in the NATO alphabet
a suspicion is a slight trace, a tad
ash is what remains after burning

explanation.surface: A student weighing fancy dress against college uniform, with a lingering doubt.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut a dash is to look stylish and striking, as someone in showy clothes does.

clue.text: Jumbo Brown, in cup matches, completely loses it!

indicators.note: in places the colour inside the word for the matches

parts.note: cup matches are ties, games in a knockout competition
tan is a brown colour

indicators.note: loses means the word it is taken out

parts.note: completely means quite, as in quite right

explanation.surface: A person named Jumbo Brown losing his temper during cup games.
explanation.walkthrough: Jumbo and Brown look like a name, but Jumbo is the definition. 'Loses it' takes IT out of QUITE, leaving QUE.
explanation.definitionFit: Titanesque means gigantic, like a Titan, and jumbo likewise means enormous in size.

clue.text: A rare pleasure left us going around by railway

indicators.note: going around means the pair surrounds the letter for by

parts.note: us is read as two yous, U and U
X is by, as in 3 by 4 for multiplication

explanation.surface: A rare treat: a railway trip that took us round in circles.
explanation.walkthrough: Us is taken as you plus you, two U's, which go around X.
explanation.definitionFit: A luxury is an indulgence enjoyed only now and then, something that gives special pleasure.

clue.text: See 7
See 8
Had exotic masala rather than a cold meal

indicators.note: exotic means unusual or foreign, so the remaining letters are rearranged
rather than says the letter a is to be left out of the mix of had and masala

explanation.surface: Someone ate a spicy curry dish instead of a plain cold lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: Setter's intent: the jumbled masala takes the place of the A in Had, so the two words share their letters less one A.
explanation.definitionFit: A ham salad is a classic British cold lunch of sliced cured pork with salad leaves.

clue.text: Hero of novel chapter one eats in Burma

definitions.note: eats is a colloquial noun for food, matching a dish

parts.note: Kim is the boy hero of Rudyard Kipling's novel Kim
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: The novel's hero, in chapter one, dines in Burma.
explanation.walkthrough: Kimchi is in fact Korean; the Burma link is loose, perhaps an echo of Kipling's Asian settings.
explanation.definitionFit: Kimchi is a spicy fermented cabbage dish from Korea, so it is food from Asia rather than strictly Burmese fare.

clue.text: Liqueurs knocked back in USA if at a reunion

indicators.note: knocked back says the hidden letters are read backwards
in says the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Drinks downed at an American reunion.
explanation.definitionFit: Ratafia is a sweet almond or fruit-kernel flavoured cordial, a kind of liqueur.

clue.text: It's unlikely her hits will work as Sweet covers

indicators.note: covers means the word for sweet wraps around everything else

parts.note: a pet is a sweet, dear person

indicators.note: will work means the letters of her hits are worked into a new order

parts.note: as and though can both introduce a concession, as in try as I might

explanation.surface: The band Sweet recording cover versions of a singer's hits is unlikely to succeed.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweet suggests the 1970s glam band, but it is PET, wrapping RISHTHE (from 'her hits') plus THOUGH.
explanation.definitionFit: Perish the thought is an idiom dismissing an idea as not going to happen or not to be wished for.
